title: Coherent nerve compares simplicial categories with infinity categories
statement:
Use simplicial sets [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set], quasicategories, Kan complexes, weak homotopy equivalences and mapping spaces [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], in sufficiently large fixed universes. A small simplicial category $A$ has a set of objects, simplicial mapping sets $A(x,y)$, identity vertices and associative unital simplicial composition maps. Its category $\pi_0A$ has the same objects and the components of its mapping sets as morphisms. A Dwyer--Kan equivalence is a simplicial functor inducing weak homotopy equivalences on all mapping sets and an equivalence on $\pi_0$. The category $\mathrm{sCat}$ of small simplicial categories has the Bergner model structure, whose weak equivalences are these functors. Fibrations are local Kan fibrations with the following equivalence-lifting property: every isomorphism in $\pi_0$ of the target with source the image of an object lifts to an isomorphism in $\pi_0$ of the source with that source. Cofibrations are the maps with the left lifting property against trivial fibrations. Trivial means also a weak equivalence; cofibrant means that the initial map is a cofibration. There is a functorial locally Kan replacement $A\to RA$ fixing its objects and inducing weak homotopy equivalences on every mapping set. The replacement may be chosen to fix discrete simplicial categories and their maps.

For each $n$, let $\mathfrak C[\Delta^n]$ have objects $0,\ldots,n$ and, for $i\leq j$, mapping set the ordinary nerve of the poset of subsets of $\{i,\ldots,j\}$ containing $i,j$, ordered by inclusion; for $i>j$ the mapping set is empty. Composition is union of subsets. Set $N_{\mathrm{hc}}(A)_n=\operatorname{Fun}_{\mathrm{sCat}}(\mathfrak C[\Delta^n],A)$, with operators induced by monotone maps, and extend $\mathfrak C$ to simplicial sets by colimits over their simplices. The adjunction $\mathfrak C\dashv N_{\mathrm{hc}}$ is a Quillen equivalence from the Joyal model structure on simplicial sets to the Bergner model structure. In the Joyal structure cofibrations are monomorphisms and fibrant objects are quasicategories. The derived functor $\mathbf RN_{\mathrm{hc}}(A)=N_{\mathrm{hc}}(RA)$ identifies the homotopy theory of simplicial categories with $\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$, the infinity category of small quasicategories and functors. This identification carries homotopy pushout diagrams to pushout diagrams in $\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$. On an ordinary category with discrete mapping sets the coherent nerve is its ordinary nerve. For every locally Kan $A$, the coherent nerve is a quasicategory, and there are natural equivalences of spaces
$$A(x,y)\simeq\operatorname{Map}_{N_{\mathrm{hc}}A}(x,y).$$
These are induced by the coherent-nerve adjunction, send a vertex of $A(x,y)$ to its corresponding edge, and preserve enriched composition with its coherent homotopies. If $A$ is locally Kan and $\pi_0A$ is a groupoid, $N_{\mathrm{hc}}A$ is Kan. All comparisons are natural for simplicial functors.

proof.text: Construct $\mathfrak C$ from the displayed subset posets and simplex colimits. For any $S,A$, maps $\mathfrak C[S]\to A$ are compatible families of maps $\mathfrak C[\Delta^n]\to A$ indexed by simplices of $S$, hence exactly maps $S\to N_{\mathrm{hc}}A$. Restriction along monotone maps gives the faces and degeneracies, so this bijection is natural and gives the adjunction. Its unit and counit are the compatible evaluation maps; the triangle identities say that evaluating a represented simplex returns that simplex. This uses precisely the construction of $\mathfrak C$ in the rigidification input, not an assumed adjunction equivalence.

source.place: Section 1.1.5, definition of the coherent nerve and coherent realization; simplex-colimit adjunction.

proof.text: Write $W$ for the Dwyer--Kan equivalences, and $F=J\text{-inj}$ for the class identified in the interval-lifting input. Its vertexwise equivalence-lifting condition agrees with the statement's $\pi_0$ condition. Indeed a vertex representing a given invertible component exists by the definition of components. A lift in $\pi_0$ gives a lifted vertex whose image is in the same component as the prescribed vertex. Join them by a finite zigzag of $1$-simplices; local Kan fibrations lift each edge with either endpoint prescribed, using the two $1$-horns. The resulting vertex is still invertible in $\pi_0$ and maps to the prescribed vertex exactly. The reverse implication follows by taking components. No Kan condition on $A$ or $B$ is being assumed here.

source.place: Section 2, Propositions 2.3 and 2.5; comparison of (F2) with the component formulation.

proof.text: A map is $I\text{-inj}$ exactly when it is surjective on objects and a trivial Kan fibration on each mapping set: the nullary object generator tests surjectivity and the $U$-boundary generators test the mapping-set lifting problems, including $\partial\Delta^0=\varnothing$. Such a map is in $W\cap F$: it is locally a weak equivalence, its $\pi_0$ is fully faithful and surjective on objects, and every target equivalence lifts by local surjectivity on vertices; full faithfulness makes that lift invertible. Conversely, $p\in W\cap F$ is locally a trivial Kan fibration by the Kan--Quillen structure. Essential surjectivity of $\pi_0p$, followed by equivalence lifting in $F$, makes $p$ strictly surjective on objects. Therefore $I\text{-inj}=W\cap F$.

The interval inputs supply the two small-object weak factorization systems, $J\text{-cof}\subset I\text{-cof}$, and $J\text{-cof}\subset W$ (relative $J$-cells are in $W$ and $W$ is retract closed). If $f\in I\text{-cof}\cap W$, factor $f=pj$ with $j\in J\text{-cell}$ and $p\in F$. Two-out-of-three gives $p\in W$, so step 3 gives $p\in I\text{-inj}$. The lifting square with top $j$, left $f$, right $p$ and bottom the identity makes $f$ a retract of $j$ in the arrow category. Thus $J\text{-cof}=I\text{-cof}\cap W$. Together with step 3, these are exactly the two model weak factorization systems. Completeness, cocompleteness and the retract/two-out-of-three axioms are in the cited inputs. This constructs the Bergner structure with the required classes; its underlying category is locally presentable and both systems are set generated, so it is combinatorial. Finally $A\to *$ is in $F$ exactly when all its mapping sets are Kan: the remaining equivalence to lift in $*$ is the identity and is lifted by an identity of $A$.

source.place: Section 3, model-structure proof from Propositions 3.1–3.3 and Lemma 3.4.

proof.text: Apply $\operatorname{Ex}^{\infty}$ separately to all mapping sets, keeping the object set. Define composition by the inverse canonical product comparison followed by $\operatorname{Ex}^{\infty}$ of the old composition, and use its terminal comparison for identities. The product comparisons commute with projections, so their two iterated versions agree; applying the old associativity and identity equations proves the new ones. Naturality gives $A\to RA$ as a simplicial functor and makes $R$ functorial. The Ex input gives locally Kan mapping sets and local weak equivalences. For a discrete set $D$, every map from $\operatorname{Sd}\Delta^n$ to $D$ is constant, because that subset poset is nonempty and connected (its full subset is terminal); hence $\operatorname{Ex}D=D$ canonically, as is the iterated colimit, with unit the identity. Normalize using these canonical identifications. Thus $R$ fixes discrete categories and maps, including empty mapping sets and the empty category.

source.place: Construction 3.3.6.1; Propositions 3.3.6.4, 3.3.6.7 and 3.3.6.9; productwise enriched construction.

proof.text: The functor $\mathfrak C$ sends monomorphisms to $I\text{-cof}$ maps. It suffices to check simplex boundaries, since every simplicial monomorphism has the boundary-cell expression in the Kan--Quillen input and $\mathfrak C$ preserves colimits. For $n=0$ the image adds one object. For $n>0$, the subset-poset formula shows that $\mathfrak C[\partial\Delta^n]\to\mathfrak C[\Delta^n]$ is the pushout of $U(\partial(\Delta^1)^{n-1})\to U((\Delta^1)^{n-1})$: all mapping sets except $(0,n)$ agree, and in that mapping set the boundary is the union of faces obtained either by omitting an interior vertex or by requiring it. The latter are the composites through that vertex. The boundary of the zero-dimensional cube for $n=1$ is empty. Cube-boundary inclusion is a simplicial monomorphism, hence a boundary-cell map, so its $U$ image is $I\text{-cof}$. To see this last assertion without assuming $U$ preserves arbitrary enriched colimits, test lifts: lifting against $U(K)\to U(L)$ with a fixed choice of the two objects is precisely lifting $K\to L$ in that one mapping set. Therefore each map against which all $U$-boundaries lift also lifts this $U$-monomorphism. This proves the claimed cofibration preservation.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 2.2.5.1, verification (C), cube boundary description.

proof.text: By the rigidification detection criterion, $\mathfrak C$ sends every categorical equivalence, in particular every Joyal trivial cofibration, to $W$. Step 6 sends its cofibration part to $I\text{-cof}$, so the adjunction of step 1 is Quillen. A right adjoint in a Quillen pair takes fibrant objects to fibrant objects: adjoint a lifting square against any trivial cofibration, then lift against $A\to *$. Using the fibrant characterizations in step 4 and in the Joyal input, a locally Kan $A$ therefore has $N_{\mathrm{hc}}A$ a quasicategory. This establishes the hypothesis needed for the pinched comparison in the next step before applying that comparison.

For locally Kan $A$, write $S=N_{\mathrm{hc}}A$. An $n$-simplex in $\operatorname{Map}^{R}_{S}(x,y)$ is an enriched functor $\mathfrak C[J^n]\to A$ with endpoints fixed, by step 1. The collapsed-face construction says its only nonidentity mapping input is $Q^n$, so this is a map $Q^n\to A(x,y)$. These identifications commute with all operators: $\operatorname{Map}^{R}_{S}(x,y)=\operatorname{Sing}_Q A(x,y)$. On each copy of $Q^n$, the composite of $\theta_{S,x,y}$ with the enriched counit $\varepsilon_A:\mathfrak C[N_{\mathrm{hc}}A]\to A$ is evaluation of that functor. Thus it is the evaluation map $e_{A(x,y)}$. Both $\theta$ and $e$ are weak equivalences by the pinched-resolution input, since $S$ is a quasicategory and $A(x,y)$ is Kan. Two-out-of-three proves that $\varepsilon_A$ is a local weak equivalence. It is the identity on objects, hence a Dwyer--Kan equivalence.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 2.2.0.1 using Proposition 2.2.4.1 and Corollary 2.2.2.10.

proof.text: Every simplicial set $T$ is Joyal cofibrant. For fibrant $A$ and a map $u:T\to N_{\mathrm{hc}}A$, its adjunct is $v=\varepsilon_A\mathfrak C[u]$. Step 8 makes $\varepsilon_A$ a Dwyer--Kan equivalence, so two-out-of-three and detection give: $v$ is a Dwyer--Kan equivalence if and only if $\mathfrak C[u]$ is, if and only if $u$ is a categorical equivalence. This is the cofibrant-source/fibrant-target criterion defining a Quillen equivalence. It proves the claimed Quillen equivalence from its adjunction, detection and counit, rather than assuming it as another node.

For clarity the equivalence retains the entire localized infinity categories. Coherent localization means the universal property on functor infinity categories in the model-colimit input. The functor $\mathfrak C$ preserves weak equivalences by detection. If $f:A\to B$ is in $W$, naturality of $A\to RA$ and two-out-of-three give $Rf\in W$. Apply naturality of the weakly equivalent counits from step 8 to $RA,RB$; this makes $\mathfrak C[N_{\mathrm{hc}}Rf]$ a Dwyer--Kan equivalence, and detection makes $N_{\mathrm{hc}}Rf$ a categorical equivalence. Consequently $N_{\mathrm{hc}}R$ also descends to coherent localization. For each $T$, let $\eta'_T:T\to N_{\mathrm{hc}}R\mathfrak C[T]$ be adjunct to $\mathfrak C[T]\to R\mathfrak C[T]$. Its composite $\varepsilon_{R\mathfrak C[T]}\mathfrak C[\eta'_T]$ is that local weak equivalence. Detection and step 8 imply that $\eta'_T$ is a categorical equivalence. On simplicial categories the natural zigzag $\mathfrak C[N_{\mathrm{hc}}RA]\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_{RA}}RA\leftarrow A$ has both arrows in $W$. By the enhanced calculus, their pointwise equivalence components are equivalences in the functor quasicategories. The localization universal property identifies whole functor infinity categories with the full subcategories of weak-equivalence-inverting functors, so these unit and counit zigzags descend to natural equivalences; they exhibit inverse infinity functors. With $\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$ modeled by the homotopy coherent localization of the Joyal model category (whose objects can be represented by its fibrant quasicategories), the inverse comparison is exactly $A\mapsto N_{\mathrm{hc}}RA$.

source.place: Theorem 2.2.5.1, localized interpretation; explicit relative-functor unit and counit argument.

proof.text: The model-colimit comparison applies to $\mathrm{sCat}$ because step 4 proved combinatoriality, in the same fixed universes. Apply it to the small ordinary span shape and a projectively cofibrant replacement of any given span. Its colimit cocone becomes a pushout in the coherent localization of $\mathrm{sCat}$. A homotopy pushout cocone differs from this by the stipulated weak equivalence of apices, so it too becomes a pushout. The equivalence in step 10 preserves this property: a cocone with apex $P$ is colimiting precisely when its mapping space into every $E$ is the corresponding limit of mapping spaces, and an equivalence identifies every mapping space and every $E$ up to equivalence. Hence $\mathbf RN_{\mathrm{hc}}$ carries the whole homotopy pushout cocone to a pushout cocone in $\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$, with its maps.

source.place: Theorem 7.9.8 and Remark 7.9.10, duals; span specialization and cocone universal property.

proof.text:
For locally Kan $A$, step 8 and the pinched-resolution input give the natural zigzag of weak equivalences
$$A(x,y)\xleftarrow{e_{A(x,y)}}|\operatorname{Sing}_QA(x,y)|_Q=|\operatorname{Map}^{R}_{N_{\mathrm{hc}}A}(x,y)|_Q\xrightarrow{p}\operatorname{Map}^{R}_{N_{\mathrm{hc}}A}(x,y).$$
The right mapping space is Kan by the enhanced calculus, and the left end is Kan by the local Kan hypothesis. Both ends are spaces, so this is the asserted equivalence of mapping spaces. As $Q^0=\Delta^0$, its action on a vertex is its corresponding edge. Compatibility with composition uses the actual counit, not only the fact that these spaces have the same homotopy type: the evaluation composite in step 8 is the map of mapping sets of the enriched functor $\varepsilon_A$, which preserves composition strictly. On a simplex $\mathfrak C[\Delta^n]\to A$, its values on the subset cubes specify all composites, and the edges adding an intermediate vertex specify the homotopies from a long arrow to the corresponding composite. Restricting to faces gives the lower coherence relations, and composition in the cubes is union of subsets, so all higher compatibility relations are preserved by evaluation. The map $p$ and its degree-zero identity are natural in these restrictions. Thus the equivalence induced by the coherent-nerve adjunction respects enriched composition with these coherent homotopies. All formulas commute with enriched functors $A\to B$.

source.place: Sections 1.1.5, 2.2.2 and 2.2.4; comparison via the enriched evaluation counit.

proof.text: For a discrete simplicial category, every map from a subset-poset nerve to a discrete mapping set is constant, since the poset has a least and a greatest element. Therefore a functor $\mathfrak C[\Delta^n]\to A$ is uniquely a string of $n$ composable arrows in its ordinary category: the image on $(i,j)$ is forced to be the composite of the adjacent arrows by union composition. Faces compose adjacent arrows, degeneracies insert identities. Hence $N_{\mathrm{hc}}A$ is its ordinary nerve, naturally also on functors. The empty category has the empty nerve by the same simplex definition.

Let $f:x\to y$ be a vertex of $A(x,y)$ with $A$ locally Kan and $\pi_0A$ a groupoid. Choose a vertex $g:y\to x$ representing its inverse component. Then $gf$ and $1_x$ lie in the same component of the Kan complex $A(x,x)$, as do $fg$ and $1_y$ in $A(y,y)$. In a Kan complex a finite edge zigzag can be reversed and concatenated into one edge: fill a $2$-horn with one edge and a degenerate edge to reverse an edge, and an inner $2$-horn to concatenate two. Hence there are edges $1_x\to gf$ and $1_y\to fg$. The first edge, together with $f,g$, defines an enriched functor $\mathfrak C[\Delta^2]\to A$ with objects $x,y,x$: its sole nonconstant mapping cube is $\Delta^1$, with initial vertex the long edge $1_x$ and final vertex the forced composite $gf$. This is a $2$-simplex of $N_{\mathrm{hc}}A$ witnessing one inverse equation. The second edge gives the other inverse triangle on $y,x,y$. Every edge of the coherent nerve is a vertex in an enriched mapping set by the displayed formula for $\mathfrak C[\Delta^1]$, so all its edges are equivalences in the definition's inverse-triangle sense. Its core is therefore its whole simplicial set. Step 7 established that it is a quasicategory, and the enhanced calculus says that its core is Kan. Thus $N_{\mathrm{hc}}A$ is Kan. The comparisons in the statement are natural because objectwise Ex, simplex restriction, the adjunction and evaluation all commute with simplicial functors; the inverse choices here certify a property and are not extra comparison data.
